title: Project Layout & Clean Architecture
summary: **Project layout** and **clean architecture** are about *where code lives* and *which way dependencies point*. The core rule is simple: inner layers (your domain) must not import outer layers (HTTP, databases). You enforce it with **interfaces (ports)** defined by the consumer, concrete **adapters** that implement them, and a **composition root** in `cmd/` that wires everything together. Go favors simplicity — start flat and add structure only when the pain demands it.

subtopics.title: The standard project-layout (and why it's not official)
subtopics.explanation: The popular golang-standards/project-layout repo suggests /cmd (one dir per binary's main), /internal (compiler-private packages), /pkg (exportable libraries), /api, /configs. It is a community convention, NOT endorsed by the Go team — especially /pkg, which is controversial. Treat it as a menu, not a mandate. Most services need far less.

subtopics.title: internal/ is compiler-enforced privacy
subtopics.explanation: Any package under an internal/ directory can only be imported by code rooted at internal/'s parent. The compiler rejects imports from outside that subtree. It's the only access control Go gives you beyond exported/unexported identifiers — perfect for keeping implementation packages from leaking into your public API.
subtopics.example:
// only myapp/... can import this
myapp/internal/storage/postgres

subtopics.title: The Dependency Rule
subtopics.explanation: Source-code dependencies point inward only. The domain (entities, use cases) knows nothing about HTTP, SQL, or JSON. Outer layers depend on inner layers, never the reverse. This is what makes the core testable and swappable: you can replace Postgres with an in-memory map without touching domain logic.
subtopics.example:
// domain imports nothing infrastructural
package order // no import of "database/sql"

subtopics.title: Ports & adapters (interfaces)
subtopics.explanation: A 'port' is an interface the inner layer needs (e.g. OrderRepository). An 'adapter' is an outer-layer type that implements it (a Postgres repo, an in-memory fake). The inner layer depends on the abstract port; the concrete adapter is injected at startup. This is the seam that decouples your logic from infrastructure.
subtopics.example: type Repo interface{ Save(o Order) error }

subtopics.title: Define interfaces where they are USED
subtopics.explanation: A key Go idiom: the consumer declares the interface it needs, with only the methods it actually calls. Don't define a giant interface next to the implementation. 'Accept interfaces, return structs' — functions take small interfaces and return concrete types, which keeps coupling low and interfaces minimal.
subtopics.example:
// service.go (consumer) owns the interface
type repo interface{ ByID(id int) (Order, error) }

subtopics.title: The composition root (cmd/)
subtopics.explanation: All concrete wiring happens in one place — usually main() in cmd/. That's where you open the database, build the concrete adapter, inject it into the service, attach HTTP handlers, and start the server. The composition root is the only package that's allowed to know about every concrete type.

foundations.overview: When a Go service is young, it can — and should — be a single flat package. As it grows, two questions decide whether it stays maintainable: where does each piece of code live, and which way do dependencies flow? Clean architecture (a relative of hexagonal / ports-and-adapters) answers the second question with one rule: source-code dependencies always point inward, toward your business logic, never outward toward HTTP or databases. Project layout answers the first: a small, conventional set of directories (cmd, internal, and a few packages named for what they provide) that map cleanly onto that dependency flow. Go's tooling even enforces part of this for you via the internal/ directory.
foundations.formalDefinition: Clean architecture organizes code into concentric layers (entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks/drivers) governed by the Dependency Rule: a source-code dependency may only point inward, so inner layers are unaware of outer ones. Project layout is the physical mapping of those layers onto Go packages and directories, using interfaces (ports) defined by inner layers and implemented by outer adapters, with all concrete wiring confined to a composition root.
foundations.whyItMatters: Get dependency direction right and your core logic becomes trivially testable (swap a real database for an in-memory fake), your infrastructure becomes swappable, and changes stay local. Get it wrong — a domain package importing your SQL layer — and you get tangled imports, slow tests that need a real database, and eventually an import cycle the compiler flat-out refuses to build.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture an onion. The center is your business rules — pure Go, no imports of anything I/O. Each outer ring (use cases, then adapters, then HTTP/DB frameworks) may reach inward to use the ring beneath it, but an inner ring can never reach outward. To let the core talk to the outside, the core defines a small interface (a port) and the outer ring 'plugs in' a concrete implementation (an adapter). The plug, not the socket, knows the details.
foundations.runtimePerspective: There is no runtime layer here — these are compile-time, source-level constraints. The Go compiler enforces two of them directly: it refuses to compile an import cycle (a hard error), and it refuses to let code outside an internal/ tree import packages within it. Interface dispatch (a port call) costs a small indirect call through an itable, negligible versus the I/O it usually fronts. The architecture is paid for at build time, not run time.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A typical Go web service: cmd/api/main.go wires dependencies; internal/order holds the domain type and a Service with business rules plus the OrderRepository interface it needs; internal/storage/postgres implements that interface; internal/http translates requests into service calls. Tests for the service use an in-memory fake repo, so they run in microseconds with no database.
foundations.businessImpact: Testable, decoupled cores ship features faster and break less. Swappable adapters mean you can migrate from one database or message broker to another without rewriting business logic, protecting against vendor lock-in and de-risking infrastructure changes.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Clear layering lets large teams work in parallel with minimal merge conflicts, makes onboarding faster (the structure tells the story), and turns slow integration-only test suites into fast unit tests that exercise the core through fakes.
foundations.performanceImpact: Architectural boundaries are essentially free at runtime — an interface call is one indirect jump. The real performance lever is that fast, fake-backed unit tests give tight feedback loops, but beware over-abstraction: an interface per struct with one implementation adds indirection and cognitive cost for no benefit.
commonUseCases: Web/API services split into domain, storage, and transport packages
Swapping a real database adapter for an in-memory fake in tests
Hiding implementation packages behind internal/ so they can't leak into a public API
A single cmd/ composition root wiring concrete adapters into the domain

commonMisconceptions.myth: golang-standards/project-layout is the official Go layout.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is a community convention, not endorsed by the Go team. The /pkg directory in particular is controversial; start flat and add structure only when you feel real pain.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every struct should have a corresponding interface.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Interfaces belong where they're consumed and should be small. An interface with one implementation and one caller usually just adds indirection — 'accept interfaces, return structs', and only abstract a seam you actually need to swap or test.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Clean architecture means lots of layers and folders up front.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go favors simplicity. A small service can be two or three packages. Layers are a tool for managing dependency direction, not a checklist of mandatory folders.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Interfaces should be defined next to their implementation, like in Java.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Idiomatic Go defines interfaces where they are USED (the consumer), listing only the methods that caller needs. The implementer just satisfies it structurally — no 'implements' keyword required.

visualExplorer.title: The Dependency Rule, layer by layer
visualExplorer.caption: Source-code dependencies point inward. Each outer layer may use the one inside it; an inner layer never imports an outer one.

config.intro: From the pure core outward — and which way the arrows are allowed to point:

steps.name: Entities (innermost)
steps.detail: Pure domain types and rules (e.g. Order, with validation). Import nothing infrastructural — no database/sql, no net/http, no JSON tags driving behavior.

steps.name: Use cases
steps.detail: Application logic / services that orchestrate entities. They define the PORTS (interfaces like OrderRepository) they need, but depend only on entities and those abstract ports.

steps.name: Interface adapters
steps.detail: Concrete ADAPTERS that implement the ports: a Postgres repository, an HTTP handler translating requests into use-case calls. They depend inward on use cases and entities.

steps.name: Frameworks & drivers (outermost)
steps.detail: The database driver, web framework, message broker. Pure detail. The core never imports these; they are plugged in from the edge.

steps.name: Composition root wires it
steps.detail: cmd/main.go is the only place that knows every concrete type: it builds adapters and injects them inward, so dependencies still point the right way.

visualExplorer.title: A port is just an interface
visualExplorer.caption: The use case depends on an abstract Repository (the port). A real Postgres adapter and an in-memory fake both satisfy it — so the core never changes when infrastructure does.

interactiveExamples.title: The ports-and-adapters seam in one file
interactiveExamples.explanation: The domain Service depends on a small Repository interface (the port). main() injects an in-memory adapter that satisfies it. Notice the Service never mentions a map, a database, or JSON — it only knows the port. Swapping in a real database means writing another adapter, not touching the Service.

code.expectedOutput:
rejected: order total must be positive
order 1 placed for 4200 cents

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: define the port at the consumer, not the implementation
interactiveExamples.explanation: Right now the service references a concrete *PostgresRepo (simulated), so it can't be tested without that exact type. Refactor it to depend on a small interface declared next to the consumer, then inject the fake. The goal: PlaceOrder works with ANY type that has Save, proving the seam.

checkpoints.prompt: An in-memory adapter is injected into a service. What does this print?
options: compile error: mem does not implement Repo
checkpoints.explanation: mem has a Get method, so it structurally satisfies the Repo interface — no 'implements' keyword needed. lookup accepts the interface, calls Get("id"), and returns the value "A1". This is the ports-and-adapters seam in miniature: lookup depends on the abstraction, not on map.

checkpoints.prompt: Following idiomatic Go and the Dependency Rule, where should the OrderRepository interface be defined?
options: In the postgres package, next to the concrete implementation
In the domain/use-case package that consumes it, listing only the methods it calls
In a shared 'interfaces' or 'common' package that everything imports
In package main, so the composition root owns it
checkpoints.explanation: Idiomatic Go defines interfaces at the consumer, keeping them small. That way the inner use-case layer owns its port and depends on nothing outward; the outer postgres adapter just satisfies it structurally. Putting it next to the implementation (option A) inverts the dependency, and 'common' packages (option C) are an anti-pattern that creates wide coupling.

checkpoints.prompt: This won't compile. What's the architectural bug?
options: The two packages import each other — an import cycle, which Go forbids; dependencies also point the wrong way
checkpoints.explanation: order imports storage and storage imports order — a circular import, which the Go compiler rejects outright. It's also a dependency-direction violation: the domain (order) should not depend on the storage layer at all. Fix it by having order define a small repository interface that storage implements, so dependencies point inward only.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the directory whose contents the Go compiler will refuse to let other modules import.
checkpoints.explanation: The internal/ directory is special to the compiler: packages under it can only be imported by code rooted at internal/'s parent. /pkg is just a convention with no enforcement, and 'private'/'lib' have no special meaning in Go.

codeLab.title: Prove the seam: a service against a repository port
codeLab.instructions: In package solution, implement a Wallet domain with a Service that depends on the consumer-defined Balances interface (a port). Service.Deposit(id, amount) must reject non-positive amounts with an error and otherwise add to the balance via the port. Because Service depends only on the interface, the test injects an in-memory fake — proving the seam is testable with no real database.
hints: NewService should store the injected interface value: &Service{store: b}.
Deposit validates amount > 0 first; return an error from the errors package otherwise.
Balance and Deposit both delegate to the port (s.store.Get / s.store.Add) — the Service never knows the concrete store type, which is exactly why the fake works.

debuggingLab.title: import cycle not allowed
debuggingLab.symptom: The build fails with 'import cycle not allowed' between the domain package and the storage package.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: user imports storage and storage imports user, forming a cycle the Go compiler refuses to build. The deeper problem is dependency DIRECTION: the domain (user) should not depend on the storage layer. The fix is to invert the dependency — have the inner layer define a small interface (port) that the outer storage layer implements. Then user depends only on its own abstraction, and storage depends inward on user. The cycle disappears because the arrows now point one way.
commonMistakes: Breaking the cycle by merging both packages into one — it compiles but throws away the layering entirely.
Moving the User type into storage so the domain depends on the database layer — that's the dependency direction backwards.
Defining the repository interface inside the storage package, which keeps the domain importing storage.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the user package define a Repository interface it needs, depend on that, and let storage implement it — so no package imports outward.

theory.question: What is the Dependency Rule in clean architecture, and how do you implement it in Go?
theory.directAnswer: The Dependency Rule says source-code dependencies may only point inward, toward the business core: inner layers (entities, use cases) must not import outer layers (HTTP, databases). In Go you implement it by having the inner layer define small interfaces (ports) for what it needs, the outer layer provide concrete types that satisfy those interfaces (adapters), and a composition root in cmd/ inject the adapters inward. The compiler also helps by forbidding import cycles and enforcing internal/ boundaries.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A compile-time constraint on which packages may import which, keeping business logic independent of infrastructure.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So the core is testable and infrastructure is swappable: you can replace the database or transport without touching domain logic, and test the domain with fast in-memory fakes.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Inner layers declare interfaces (ports); outer layers implement them (adapters); dependencies are injected at a single composition root, so every source-level arrow points inward.

theory.whyImportant: It's the single idea that separates a maintainable layered service from a tangled ball of mutual imports, and it directly enables fast unit testing — a frequent senior interview topic.
theory.realWorldExample: An OrderService depends on an OrderRepository interface it defines; production wires in a Postgres adapter, tests wire in an in-memory map — the service code is identical in both.

followUps.question: How does Go enforce part of this for you?
followUps.answer: It refuses to compile import cycles, and the internal/ directory restricts imports to the subtree rooted at internal/'s parent, preventing implementation packages from leaking outward.

followUps.question: Where should the port interface live?
followUps.answer: At the consumer (the inner use-case package), listing only the methods that caller uses — not next to the implementation.

theory.question: Explain the golang-standards/project-layout: what are cmd/, internal/, and pkg/, and how official is it?
theory.directAnswer: It's a community convention, NOT endorsed by the Go team. /cmd holds main packages, one directory per binary, kept thin (just wiring). /internal holds private packages the compiler prevents other modules from importing. /pkg is meant for library code you intend others to import — but it's controversial and often unnecessary. The honest advice is to start flat and add directories only when the project genuinely needs them.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A popular GitHub repository proposing a directory structure for Go projects.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To give larger projects a shared vocabulary for where code lives, especially the genuinely useful cmd/ and internal/ conventions.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: cmd/<name>/main.go is each binary's entrypoint; internal/ is compiler-enforced privacy; pkg/ is a convention with no special meaning to the toolchain.

theory.whyImportant: Interviewers probe whether you cargo-cult enterprise structure or understand that Go favors simplicity and only cmd//internal/ carry real weight.
theory.realWorldExample: A small service might be just main.go plus a couple of packages; a larger one uses cmd/api, cmd/worker, and internal/ subpackages, and skips /pkg entirely.

followUps.question: Why is /pkg controversial?
followUps.answer: It has no compiler meaning, adds a level of nesting, and many maintainers (and the Go team) see it as unnecessary ceremony — exported packages already signal 'public'.

followUps.question: What does internal/ actually enforce?
followUps.answer: Packages under internal/ can only be imported by code rooted at internal/'s parent directory; anything outside that subtree gets a compile error.

scenario.question: Your team's domain package imports the database package so tests need a real Postgres, making the suite slow and flaky. How do you refactor for fast, isolated tests without rewriting business logic?
scenario.directAnswer: Invert the dependency: have the domain define a small repository interface (a port) for exactly the operations it uses, depend on that interface, and move the Postgres code into an adapter package that implements it. Inject the concrete adapter from the composition root in cmd/. Now the domain imports nothing infrastructural, so tests inject an in-memory fake and run in microseconds; the Postgres adapter gets a separate, smaller integration test.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A dependency inversion to put a testable seam between domain logic and persistence.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because a domain that imports the database forces every domain test to spin up that database — slow, flaky, and coupled.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The inner layer owns the interface; outer adapters satisfy it structurally; wiring happens once in main(), so domain tests never touch real infrastructure.

scenario.whyImportant: Slow, infrastructure-coupled test suites are a top productivity killer; the fix is a classic ports-and-adapters refactor that interviewers love to see reasoned through.
scenario.realWorldExample: After the refactor, OrderService_test.go uses a fakeRepo map and runs instantly, while postgres_test.go (tagged integration) is the only test that needs a database.

followUps.question: How do you keep the interface from becoming a god-object?
followUps.answer: Define it at the consumer with only the methods that caller uses; if two consumers need different methods, give each its own small interface.

followUps.question: Won't this add lots of interfaces?
followUps.answer: Only at real seams. Don't add an interface for a struct with a single implementation and no need to swap or fake it — that's over-abstraction.

coding.question: Implement a Notifier port and a Service that sends a welcome message through it, so the same Service works with an email adapter in production and a recording fake in tests. Signature: NewService(n Notifier) *Service with Welcome(name string) error.
coding.thoughtProcess: The Service should depend on an abstraction, not a concrete sender. Define a tiny Notifier interface with just Notify(msg string) error — defined at the consumer. The Service holds the interface and is constructed by injection ('accept interfaces, return structs'). Welcome formats the message and delegates to the port. Any type with a Notify method satisfies it, so a recording fake makes the Service trivially testable.
coding.lineByLine: Notifier is a one-method port declared at the consumer, so the Service depends on the smallest possible abstraction. Service holds a Notifier (interface), and NewService injects it — accepting an interface and returning a concrete *Service. Welcome builds the greeting and forwards it to s.n.Notify, never knowing whether that's email, SMS, or a fake. In tests, fakeNotifier records each message so you can assert on f.sent without sending anything; in production, EmailNotifier does the real work. Identical Service code, swapped adapter.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) plus the cost of the underlying Notify call.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) for the Service; the fake's slice is O(n) in messages recorded.

followUps.question: Why define Notifier at the consumer rather than next to EmailNotifier?
followUps.answer: It keeps the interface minimal (only Notify) and keeps dependencies pointing inward — the Service owns its port and never imports the email package.

followUps.question: How would you send to multiple notifiers?
followUps.answer: Write a multiNotifier adapter that itself holds a slice of Notifier and fans out in its Notify method — the Service stays unchanged because it still sees one Notifier.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Map layers onto packages, not the other way around: a domain/use-case package that imports nothing infrastructural, adapter packages (postgres, http) that depend inward, and a thin cmd/ composition root that wires concrete types. Keep cmd/ binaries small — open resources, build adapters, inject, start, and shut down. Use internal/ to stop implementation packages from leaking into any public surface. Resist adding /pkg or extra layers until real pain justifies them.
productionDeepDive.performance: Architectural boundaries are essentially free at runtime — an interface call is one indirect jump, negligible against the I/O it usually fronts. The payoff is in feedback loops: fake-backed unit tests run in microseconds. The trap is over-abstraction — an interface per single-implementation struct adds indirection and obscures call sites with no benefit; profile and inline (or drop the interface) where a seam earns nothing.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Define ports so adapters can be made safe independently: a repository adapter may guard internal state with a mutex or rely on a connection pool, while the domain stays oblivious. Pass context.Context as the first parameter through port methods for cancellation and deadlines, and ensure concurrent use of an injected adapter is documented as safe (most database/sql-backed adapters are).
productionDeepDive.reliability: Because adapters are swappable, you can ship a degraded in-memory or read-only adapter during an outage without touching domain logic. Centralized wiring in cmd/ makes graceful shutdown explicit (close pools, flush buffers, cancel contexts). Keep business invariants in the domain so they hold regardless of which adapter is plugged in.
productionDeepDive.observability: Wrap adapters with decorator adapters that add metrics, tracing, and logging — e.g. an instrumentedRepo that implements the same port, times each call, and delegates to the real one. Because it satisfies the port, the domain is unaware. This keeps cross-cutting concerns out of business logic and lets you add/remove instrumentation by changing wiring in cmd/.
productionDeepDive.security: internal/ prevents accidental exposure of sensitive implementation packages to external importers. Keep authorization decisions and validation in the domain so they can't be bypassed by swapping an adapter, and confine secrets (DB credentials, API keys) to the composition root where adapters are constructed, never to the domain.

caseStudies.problem: Serve HTTP without binding users to one concrete server or handler type.
caseStudies.solution: Define the http.Handler interface (ServeHTTP) as the port; any type satisfying it plugs in, and http.Server depends only on the abstraction.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Maximum flexibility and testability via a tiny interface, at the cost of a layer of indirection most users never notice.
caseStudies.lessons: A single, minimal, consumer-facing interface (Handler) is one of Go's most successful ports — small interfaces beat large ones.

caseStudies.problem: Support many databases through one API without the standard library depending on any specific driver.
caseStudies.solution: Define driver interfaces (database/sql/driver) as ports; concrete drivers (pq, mysql) are adapters registered at startup — the classic dependency inversion.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Drivers must conform to fixed interfaces, but applications swap databases without changing query code.
caseStudies.lessons: Defining the port in the inner package and letting outer drivers implement it is dependency inversion done right, at standard-library scale.

keyTakeaways: The Dependency Rule is the whole game: source-code dependencies point inward only — the domain must never import HTTP or database packages.

Implement seams with small interfaces (ports) defined at the consumer, concrete adapters that satisfy them, and a single cmd/ composition root that injects the wiring — 'accept interfaces, return structs'.
golang-standards/project-layout is a convention, not official; only cmd/ and the compiler-enforced internal/ carry real weight — start flat and add structure only when pain demands it.
Getting direction right makes the core testable with fast in-memory fakes and infrastructure swappable; getting it wrong gives you import cycles the compiler rejects and slow, coupled tests.
